# P2 — R & the Command Line {background-color="#2c3e50"}

## Where this fits

::: incremental
-   **Day 0 (optional Tuesday refresher)** — for getting everyone up and running before the core workshop
-   **Module 2 of 2** — follows **Module 1 (Computer Systems)**
-   Goal today: just enough **shell** and **R** to be productive on Day 1, not a full course
-   Pairs with the reading: [P2 — R & the Command Line](../Resources_Folder/Chapter_P2_R_and_CommandLine.html)
:::

## What you'll walk away with

::: incremental
-   Open a terminal and **move around the filesystem** with confidence
-   Create, view, move, and delete files; combine tools with **pipes & redirection**
-   Download data with `wget` / `curl`, and **get help** when stuck
-   Launch **RStudio**, assign variables, and work with vectors, data frames, and lists
-   Install and load packages; read & write data; write **tidyverse** pipelines
:::

# Part 1 — Get set up: install your tools {background-color="#2c3e50"}

## What you'll install

::: incremental
-   **R** + **RStudio** — the language and the desktop IDE you'll work in
-   **VS Code** — a second IDE, used to connect to **Talapas** over SSH
-   **Quarto** — turns the `.qmd` notebooks into rendered HTML / PDF
-   **LaTeX** (TinyTeX) — only needed for PDF output
-   The **command-line compiler tools** some R / Bioconductor packages need to build
:::

::: callout-note
**Which is which?** **R** and **LaTeX** are *languages* you write code / markup in; **Quarto** is the *publishing system* that weaves code + prose into a finished document; **RStudio** and **VS Code** are *IDEs* — the workbenches where you write, run, and (for VS Code) reach remote clusters like Talapas.
:::

## Required tools — install before Day 1

| Tool | Where to get it |
|----|----|
| **R ≥ 4.4** | [r-project.org](https://www.r-project.org) |
| **RStudio Desktop** | [posit.co/download/rstudio-desktop](https://posit.co/download/rstudio-desktop/) |
| **VS Code** | [code.visualstudio.com](https://code.visualstudio.com/download) |
| **Quarto** | [quarto.org/docs/get-started](https://quarto.org/docs/get-started/) |
| **LaTeX (TinyTeX)** | `quarto install tinytex` (only for PDF output) |

::: callout-tip
Plan **30–60 minutes the day before** — not the morning of. Full step-by-step: [Software Setup](../Software_Setup.html).
:::

## Find or install a terminal

::: panel-tabset
### macOS

Built-in **Terminal** (Applications → Utilities) runs `zsh`, a POSIX shell — nothing to install. (iTerm2 is a nicer optional upgrade.)

### Windows

Windows has no POSIX shell, so install **WSL2 + Ubuntu** from **PowerShell (Admin)**:

``` bash
wsl --install -d Ubuntu     # restart when prompted
```

Then launch **Ubuntu** from the Start menu — *that window is your terminal*.

### Linux

Use your built-in **Terminal** (`bash`). Nothing to install.
:::

## Windows: WSL2 → Ubuntu → your files

::: incremental
-   **WSL2** is the engine — a lightweight Linux VM built into Windows
-   **Ubuntu** is the Linux you actually use; launching it *is* opening your terminal
-   Your Windows drives are mounted at **`/mnt/c`** — e.g. `cd /mnt/c/Users/<you>/Desktop`
-   Your Linux files show up in File Explorer under **Linux** (or type `\\wsl$`)
-   Keep the project in your Linux home (`~`) for speed; reach over to `/mnt/c` when you need a Windows file
:::

## Install the compiler toolchain

Several R / Bioconductor packages **compile from source** the first time you install them:

::: panel-tabset
### macOS

``` bash
xcode-select --install      # clang, git, make, headers
```

### Windows

Install **Rtools** matching your R (e.g. **Rtools44** for R 4.4), for the native Windows R / RStudio.

### Linux

``` bash
sudo apt install -y build-essential gfortran
```
:::

## Install the workshop packages

::: incremental
-   The full install lives in **[Tutorial 00](../Exercise_Folder/Tutorial_00_Setup_RStudio_Packages.html)** and **Part C** of this module's tutorial — paste the block into the R console
-   First install takes **20–60 min** (it builds some packages from source) — do it **before** Day 1
-   It also pre-caches the `ifnb` dataset so Tutorial 01 starts instantly
:::

::: callout-warning
Hit an install error? The [FAQ](../FAQ.html) covers the common ones — Mac compiler errors, Bioconductor mirrors, and stale library paths.
:::

# Part 2 — The Command Line {background-color="#2c3e50"}

## Why the shell first?

::: incremental
-   The **shell** is the gateway: it runs everything else (R, aligners, HPC jobs)
-   A program that takes typed **commands** and hands them to the operating system
-   **Bash** is the shell on Mac, Linux, and Windows (via WSL)
-   You reach it through a **terminal window**
-   Bioinformatics data is big — these tools scale to gigabytes effortlessly
:::

## Anatomy of a command

``` bash
ls -l Documents
```

::: incremental
-   **Prompt** — the shell signaling it's ready for input
-   **Command** — the action (`ls`)
-   **Options / flags** — change behavior (`-l` = long format)
-   **Argument** — what it operates on (`Documents`)
:::

## How a computer is organized

::: incremental
-   A tree of **directories** (folders) and **files**
-   `/` = the **root** — holds everything else
-   `~` = your **home** directory (e.g. `/Users/yourname`)
-   A **path** is a location in the tree (`/Users/wcresko/Documents`)
-   Navigating = jumping up and down between directories
:::

## Where am I? Navigating

``` bash
pwd            # print working directory — where am I?
ls             # list contents of current directory
ls -l          # long format: sizes, dates, permissions
ls -la         # also show hidden files (start with .)
cd Documents   # change into Documents
```

::: incremental
-   `pwd` tells you where you are
-   `ls` shows what's there (`-l` long, `-a` all, `-t` by time, `-S` by size)
-   `cd` moves you around
:::

## Paths: absolute vs. relative

``` bash
cd /Users/wcresko/Documents   # absolute — full path from /
cd data                       # relative — from where I am now
cd ..                         # up one directory (parent)
cd ../scripts                 # up one, then into scripts
cd ~                          # home directory
cd -                          # back to previous directory
```

::: incremental
-   **Absolute** = full path starting at `/`
-   **Relative** = from your current location
-   `.` = here · `..` = parent · `~` = home
:::

## Making, moving, removing

``` bash
mkdir project          # make a new directory
touch notes.txt        # make a new empty file
mv notes.txt README    # rename (or move) a file
cp README README.bak   # copy a file
rm README.bak          # delete a file
rmdir project          # delete an (empty) directory
```

::: incremental
-   **The shell trusts you** — `rm` deletes immediately, no trash bin
-   Naming: avoid spaces, don't start with `-`, stick to letters/numbers/`.`/`-`/`_`
-   Use meaningful extensions (`.txt`, `.csv`, `.fasta`)
:::

## Viewing files

``` bash
cat small.txt          # dump a whole (small) file
less large.txt         # page through: space=fwd, b=back, /=search, q=quit
head data.txt          # first 10 lines
head -n 20 data.txt    # first 20 lines
tail data.txt          # last 10 lines
tail -f log.txt        # follow a growing file in real time
wc -l data.txt         # count lines
```

::: {.callout-important title="Never cat a huge file"}
A 3 GB genome will freeze your session. Use `head`, `tail`, or `less` instead.
:::

## Wildcards

``` bash
ls *.csv               # everything ending in .csv
ls sample_*.fastq      # sample_1.fastq, sample_2.fastq, ...
ls data_?.txt          # ? matches exactly one character
rm tmp_*               # careful! deletes everything matching
```

::: incremental
-   `*` matches **any number** of characters
-   `?` matches **exactly one** character
-   Lets one command act on many files at once
:::

## Pipes & redirection

``` bash
ls -l > files.txt          # > send output to a file (overwrites!)
echo "more" >> files.txt   # >> append to a file
ls /nope 2> errors.txt     # 2> capture error messages
sort names.txt | uniq      # | feed one command's output into the next
```

::: incremental
-   `>` writes to a file (**overwrites**), `>>` **appends**
-   `|` chains commands — no intermediate files needed
-   Three streams: **stdin (0)**, **stdout (1)**, **stderr (2)**
:::

## Pipes: small tools, combined

``` bash
# Count how many lines match a pattern
grep "pattern" file.txt | wc -l

# Sort, find unique values, count them, rank by frequency
cat data.csv | cut -d',' -f2 | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn

# Count sequences in a FASTA file
grep "^>" genome.fa | wc -l
```

::: incremental
-   **Unix philosophy**: small tools that each do one thing well
-   Build complex pipelines one stage at a time, checking output as you go
-   Filter early to keep the data flowing through small
:::

## Downloading data

::: panel-tabset
### wget

``` bash
wget https://example.org/genome.fna.gz
```

### curl

``` bash
curl -o genome.fa.gz https://example.org/genome.fna.gz
```

### Notes

-   Both download files from a URL
-   `curl -o` lets you name the saved file
-   `.gz` = compressed — work with it directly via `zcat`, `zless`, `zgrep`
:::

## Getting help

``` bash
man ls          # full manual page (q to quit)
ls --help       # quick usage summary
```

::: incremental
-   `man command` opens the manual; press `q` to exit
-   `command --help` gives a fast summary
-   And of course: the internet and generative AI (Claude, ChatGPT)
:::

# Part 3 — R & RStudio {background-color="#2c3e50"}

## Why R?

::: incremental
-   Powerful, flexible, **free**, runs everywhere
-   Superb data management, statistics, and graphics
-   **Reproducibility** — your scripts record exactly what you did
-   Write your own functions; huge online help and community
-   Nice front end (**RStudio**) and dynamic documents (**Quarto**)
:::

## The R interpreter & RStudio panes

::: incremental
-   **R** is the engine that runs your commands; **RStudio** is the comfortable cockpit around it
-   **Source** (top-left) — your scripts and Quarto docs you edit and save
-   **Console** (bottom-left) — where commands actually run
-   **Environment / History** (top-right) — the objects you've created
-   **Files / Plots / Packages / Help** (bottom-right) — everything else
:::

## Assignment & basic math

``` r
x <- 2          # assign with <-
x * 3           # 6
y <- x * 3      # store a result
log(x)          # built-in functions: object goes in parentheses
sqrt(16)        # 4
```

::: incremental
-   Assign with `<-`; names start with a letter; R is **case sensitive** (`x` ≠ `X`)
-   Normal math precedence (PEMDAS); parentheses control order
-   Comment with `#`
:::

## Vectors — R thinks in vectors

``` r
x <- c(2, 3, 4, 2, 1, 5)   # c() = concatenate into a vector
y <- x^2                   # operations are element-wise
mean(x); median(x); sd(x)  # built-in summaries
length(x)                  # how many elements
seq(0, 10, by = 0.5)       # a regular sequence
```

::: incremental
-   A **vector** is a list of values of one type
-   Math applies to **every element at once**
-   Types: `int`, `dbl` (numeric), `chr`, `lgl`, plus **factors** for categories
:::

## Data frames — tabular data

``` r
conc    <- factor(c("low", "high", "high", "med"))
stiff   <- c(3.4, 8.4, 3.0, 5.6)
mydata  <- data.frame(conc, stiff)

mydata$stiff        # a column by name (preferred)
mydata[, 2]         # column 2
mydata[1, ]         # row 1
mydata[mydata$stiff > 4, ]   # rows meeting a condition
```

::: incremental
-   The primary structure for tabular data; vectors become **columns**
-   `[row, column]` indexing; `$` grabs a column by name
-   `factor()` marks a column as categorical
:::

## Lists — the pocket that holds anything

``` r
experiment <- list(
  sample_id  = "donor_01_CTRL",
  age        = 42,
  cell_types = c("B cell", "CD4 T", "NK")
)

experiment$sample_id     # access a slot by name
experiment[[3]]          # the contents of the 3rd slot
```

::: incremental
-   Each slot can hold a **different kind of thing** — even another list
-   `[[ ]]` returns the *contents*; `[ ]` returns a sub-list
-   **Seurat** and **SingleCellExperiment** objects are lists under the hood
:::

## Functions

``` r
round(3.14159, 2)              # positional args — order matters
round(x = 3.14159, digits = 2) # named args — order-independent, clearer

# Define your own
cv <- function(x, na.rm = TRUE) {
  if (na.rm) x <- x[!is.na(x)]
  sd(x) / mean(x)
}
cv(c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5))
```

::: incremental
-   Use **named arguments** whenever there's ambiguity — self-documenting
-   scRNA-seq functions have long signatures, so almost everything is named
-   You'll write small helper functions all the time
:::

## Packages: `install.packages()` vs `library()`

``` r
install.packages("tidyverse")   # download & install — ONCE per machine
library(tidyverse)              # load — EVERY new R session
```

::: incremental
-   **`install.packages()`** = get it onto your computer (do once)
-   **`library()`** = make it available in this session (do every time)
-   Bioconductor packages (Seurat ecosystem, DESeq2) use `BiocManager::install()`
:::

## The tidyverse & the pipe

``` r
library(tidyverse)

result <- meta |>
  filter(nFeature_RNA > 200, nFeature_RNA < 2500) |>
  group_by(sample, cluster) |>
  summarise(n_cells = n(),
            median_umi = median(nCount_RNA),
            .groups = "drop") |>
  arrange(sample, desc(n_cells))
```

::: incremental
-   Six verbs cover most work: `filter`, `select`, `mutate`, `arrange`, `group_by`, `summarise`
-   The pipe **`|>`** chains steps — read top-to-bottom, left-to-right
-   This style appears throughout the workshop tutorials
:::

## Reading & writing data

``` r
# Read
df <- read_csv("data.csv")     # tidyverse — returns a tibble
df <- read_tsv("data.txt")     # tab-separated
df <- read.csv("data.csv")     # base R equivalent

# Write
write_csv(df, "results.csv")
```

::: incremental
-   `read_csv()` / `read_tsv()` (tidyverse) return tibbles; `read.csv()` is base R
-   Store data in plain text; keep an **untouched original**; include a header row
-   One column = one data type
:::
